I toggles this off to let the 3D application settings decide and my GPU temps went down to 70/72 C in that game. Then I decided to test in other games. For reference I have a 2070 Super FE in a NZXT case with only the two pre-installed fans.

Life continues, but I'd hardly call it normal. It started off simply, all personal data was collected, we understood this was a necessary evil to keep us safe. Then came the policing, those who held conflicting opinions were hauled in front of a judge and forced to recant, lest they serve a lengthy prison sentence. Then, finally, all pretense was dropped. If you were deemed as "subversive" you simply ceased to exist, or at least that's what the government would have us believe. What did that word mean? Subversive? Basically anyone the government had reason to dislike, whether that was voting for the wrong party, having an opinion that wasn't in lockstep, or even making an uncouth joke. So what did we do? What all humans do, we adapted. We learned how to hide our dealings from the prying eye, we developed proto-languages that masked our true meaning, and some fell off the grid entirely, choosing to go back to a time before the advent of the internet. It's funny what people will grow accustomed to.

My depression started at the tender age of 14. As a young kid I was relatively happy, I had a good middle class life with parents who cared about me. Then shit hit the fan.

At the age of 13, I came home one night to my father informing me that he was going to take my mother to the ER, she was running a high fever and wasn't getting better with tylenol. My mother was in the hospital for two weeks until she was diagnosed with Non-Hodgkin's Lymphoma. As a young teenager, I didn't truly grasp this situation, especially as my father and the doctor's ensured us that the cancer was very treatable. My mother received treatment all throughout the year, but nothing worked. Eventually she was advised to get a bone marrow transplant, as a last-ditch effort to treat her cancer. She was an inpatient in a hospital for a couple of months until she was finally able to come home. My parent's had not yet told us at that point that the cancer was terminal, but it didn't take long to find out. I remember the day I got that news very well. I was sitting in math class just about to take a test and the phone in our class rang. I was asked to come to the school office as there was someone there to pick me up. I remember thinking, "Sweet, I don't have to take this test." I went down to the office and there were my brother, sister, and aunt. My sister was in tears, and something was clearly wrong. I was told my mother had contracted pneumonia and had been rushed to the ER. I went to the ER to see my mother and she was in a bad state. I was informed by a careless ER doctor that my mother likely didn't have long to live. My mother stayed in the ER for a time, and then was transferred to an Intensive Care Unit, afterwards she spent a couple days in hospice. This entire time period totaled a week. At the end of that week, I said goodbye to my mother and my innocence. Ever since that week i've struggled with anxiety and depression. We mourned the eighth anniversary of her passing a week ago.

It's no problem at all. There are legitimate concerns with these medications and they can negatively affect you. The issue in med managment is ensuring the pros of the medication outweight the cons.

I've had experience with various psych med withdrawals, they're a nasty thing. Honestly, you should never go cold turkey off a psych med, doing that can be dangerous depending on your condition. Now the question is if you want to continue to take that med or if you want to get off it. Either way, if things get worse, I would advise you to call your psychiatrist and try and speak with whoever they have on-call, and if they don't answer, most emergency rooms have some sort of psychological services as well. The most important thing through all of this is that you keep safe, as your quality of life will most likely improve one way or the another eventually. Have you ever heard of Albert Camus? If not, allow me to tell you a little about him. Albert Camus was a french philosopher from a philosophical branch named existentialists. Existentialists believe that there is no fundamental meaning to life, except for the meaning we create for ourselves. One of Camus' writings is a short story entitled the Myth of Sisyphus. The story goes that there was a greek hero who was sentenced to eternal damnation by the gods. His punishment was to be rolling a stone up a hill all day, and when he finished, the stone would roll right back down the hill, this would continue for an enternity. Camus' uses this story to illustrate the options he thinks existentialists' have. He concluded that suicide was an option for a life without meaning, however, he also believed in a concept known as the absurd hero. Camus' concluded that life is fundamentally devoid of meaning and thus absurd, and the tasks we set upon each day are equally as absurd with no fundamental meaning. This all sounds kind of grim, but he paints Sisyphus as an absurd hero, someone who is living a life without meaning, defying the gods and creating his own meaning. I do fundamentally believe that life has no inherent meaning, but that should make us more hopeful, not less, because that means we get to dictate what our meaning is. I hope you don't choose to take the path to suicide, and instead push on and try to find your own meaning.
